documents.title: Surprisal of a single event
documents.breadcrumb: Information Theory › Surprisal and entropy › Surprisal › Surprisal of a single event
documents.text: The surprisal of a single event is minus the base-two logarithm of its probability. An event of probability one half carries one bit of surprisal; an event of probability one eighth carries three bits. Additivity over independent events forces the logarithm: the surprisal of two independent events is the sum of their surprisals. Surprisal is a property of one outcome, not of the source that produced it.

documents.title: Entropy is the average surprisal of a source
documents.breadcrumb: Information Theory › Surprisal and entropy › Entropy › Entropy is the average surprisal of a source
documents.text: Entropy is the average surprisal of a source, the expectation of minus the base-two logarithm of the probability under the distribution itself. A fair coin has entropy one bit per symbol; a biased source has less. Entropy is maximal for the uniform distribution over a finite alphabet and zero for a deterministic source. It is the floor on the average code length of any lossless code for that source.

documents.title: Gibbs inequality: the overhead is never negative
documents.breadcrumb: Information Theory › Divergence › KL divergence › Gibbs inequality
documents.text: Gibbs inequality says the KL divergence is never negative, with equality if and only if the two distributions agree everywhere. Individual terms of the divergence do go negative, because a wrong code saves bits on some symbols, but the sum cannot. The standard proof runs through Jensen inequality applied to the concave logarithm of the ratio, and it delivers the equality condition in one stroke.

documents.title: Forward versus reverse KL
documents.breadcrumb: Information Theory › Divergence › KL divergence › Forward versus reverse KL
documents.text: The divergence is asymmetric, and the two orders behave differently when a model cannot represent the truth. Forward KL is mass covering: it punishes a model that assigns no probability where the data has some, so the fitted model spreads out over every mode. Reverse KL is mode seeking: it punishes probability where the data has none, so the fitted model collapses onto one mode and ignores the rest.

documents.title: Mutual information is shared information
documents.breadcrumb: Information Theory › Channels › Mutual information › Mutual information is shared information
documents.text: Mutual information is the entropy of one variable minus its conditional entropy given the other: how much observing one variable reduces uncertainty about the second. It is symmetric, never negative, and zero exactly when the two variables are independent. Equivalently it is the divergence between the joint distribution and the product of the marginals.

documents.title: Capacity of the binary symmetric channel
documents.breadcrumb: Information Theory › Channels › Channel capacity › Capacity of the binary symmetric channel
documents.text: The capacity of a binary symmetric channel with crossover probability p is one minus the binary entropy of p, achieved by the uniform input distribution. At p equal to one half the channel carries nothing; at p equal to zero it carries one bit per use. Capacity is the maximum of the mutual information between input and output over all input distributions.

documents.title: The Kraft inequality
documents.breadcrumb: Information Theory › Coding › Prefix codes › The Kraft inequality
documents.text: The Kraft inequality states that a prefix code with codeword lengths exists precisely when the sum of two to the minus each length is at most one. Read as a budget: every codeword spends part of a unit budget, and a short codeword is expensive. The converse construction reads the budget back into a code tree, so the inequality is not merely necessary but sufficient.

documents.title: Building the Huffman tree
documents.breadcrumb: Information Theory › Coding › Huffman by hand › Building the Huffman tree
documents.text: Building the Huffman tree is repeated merging: take the two least probable symbols, merge them into one node whose probability is their sum, and put it back in the pool. Repeat until a single node remains, then read the codeword of each symbol off the path from the root. The construction is optimal among prefix codes for the given symbol probabilities.

documents.title: The typical set
documents.breadcrumb: Information Theory › Coding › Source coding theorem › The typical set
documents.text: The typical set is the collection of long sequences whose empirical log probability sits close to the entropy. The asymptotic equipartition property says almost all probability mass lands in that set, and that the set has roughly two to the entropy times length members. Numbering the typical set is therefore enough to code the source at a rate approaching its entropy.

documents.title: Cross entropy is the training objective
documents.breadcrumb: Information Theory › Machine learning › Cross entropy loss › Cross entropy is the training objective
documents.text: Training a classifier by maximum likelihood is minimising the cross entropy between the empirical label distribution and the model, which is the entropy of the data plus the divergence from the data to the model. Only the divergence term depends on the parameters, so the training objective is a divergence in disguise, measured in bits per example.

documents.title: Post processing cannot create information
documents.breadcrumb: Information Theory › Channels › Data processing inequality › Post processing cannot create information
documents.text: For a Markov chain the mutual information between the first and last variable is at most the mutual information between the first and the middle one. No function of the observation, however clever, can create information about the source that the observation did not already carry. Every layer of a network is a post processing step and can only lose.

documents.title: The rate distortion function
documents.breadcrumb: Information Theory › Lossy › Rate distortion › The rate distortion function
documents.text: The rate distortion function is the least rate that a lossy code can spend while keeping the expected distortion below a budget. It is the minimum of the mutual information between source and reconstruction over all conditional distributions meeting the distortion constraint. The curve is convex and decreasing: buying fidelity always costs rate, and the last decibel costs the most.

documents.title: Research brief: infonce (Contrastive representation learning)
documents.breadcrumb: Information Theory › Research › Research brief: infonce
documents.text: The InfoNCE objective scores one positive pair against a batch of negatives and is a lower bound on the mutual information between the two views, saturating at the logarithm of the batch size. Sources: Oord, Li and Vinyals 2018; Poole and colleagues 2019 on variational bounds. The saturation is why a contrastive bound cannot certify more than a handful of bits at realistic batch sizes.

documents.title: Canals and railroads
documents.breadcrumb: US History › The early republic › The market revolution › Canals and railroads
documents.text: The Erie Canal cut the cost of moving a ton of freight from Buffalo to New York by more than ninety percent, and the railroad network that followed carried the same logic inland. Falling transport cost is what turned isolated household production into production for a distant market.
